newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurotunnel may resume freight trains "in hours".
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel may resume freight trains "in hours".

text.p: Eurotunnel's operations manager said on Wednesday freight trains might resume links under the Channel between France and Britain within hours.

"Eurotunnel plans to resume services in several phases and as quickly as possible starting in a few hours with freight trains," operations manager Alain Bertrand told the north France radio station France-Info-Frequence Nord.
Bertrand said he hoped Eurostar passenger trains and shuttle trains carrying private cars and their passengers in the 51-km (32 mile) tunnel might start rolling again before the end of the week.
He gave no indication when shuttle trains carrying cargo lorries would resume services.
It was a fire on one such lorry-carrying shuttle train on Monday in the Channel Tunnel which unleashed a storm of criticism of much-vaunted safety systems and resulted in all traffic being suspended.

"We must make some checks before this service resumes. We must also analyse some specific points," said Bertrand who spoke as a safety commission met in Calais, northern France, to take up the issue of when services could resume.
Bertrand's statement about a swift resumption of tunnel services contradicted a statement by the French SNCF railways which indicated passenger services would not resume until next week.

An SNCF statement had said: "Taking account of the prolonged closure of the Channel Tunnel, the Eurostar (rail) service is completely suspended for an as yet undetermined period, which ought to include the weekend of November 23-24.

"SNCF asks travellers who had reserved tickets for the weekend to put off their trips," it said in a statement. Tickets for the Paris-London and Brussels-London routes would either be refunded or transferred to another date.

Operator Eurotunnel SA Plc had hoped for a partial resumption of traffic on Wednesday on the unscathed southern rail tunnel, parallel to the northern tunnel ravaged over 600 metres (yards) by Monday night's fire that injured eight people.
Eurotunnel said damage was worse than first feared with buckled tracks, cracked concrete and damage to electrical cables. Full repairs are likely to last weeks and cost millions of pounds (dollars).

The only trains running in the tunnel on Wednesday were shuttling staff -- the closure to paying clients means a loss of revenues of about a million pounds ($1.68 million) a day, a pinprick compared to the company's nine billion pounds in debts.
British media branded the tunnel a "Tunnel of Blunders". French media were generally less severe, but the daily France Soir hit out saying: "The hyper-security was a bluff."
Eurotunnel faced criticism of safety systems, which include measures to withstand earthquakes, guerrilla bombs and even intercept foxes scampering from France to rabies-free Britain.

Some of the 31 drivers aboard the train that caught fire banded together and appointed a French lawyer, Gilbert Collard, to launch legal action on Thursday to find out the extent of Eurotunnel's responsiblity for the blaze.

"I'll never go back in the tunnel again," said Denis Bracqbien, a spokesman for the group. Bracqbien, a French trucker who lives in Scotland, said the group needed legal action to help them with insurance claims for wrecked trucks.
British fire chiefs criticised the tunnel's freight transporters, where trucks are loaded onto lattice-sided wagons.
Clients with tickets have been diverted onto ferries or planes, the tunnel's arch-rivals. Some Eurostar trains ran to Calais from Paris where passengers disembarked to take ferries.
